title: Big-O Notation and Space Complexity
prompt: In your own words, explain Big-O notation and why it is important for analyzing algorithms. Then analyze the following function: while (n > 1) { n = n / 2; }. State its time complexity and space complexity, and explain how the time complexity would change if each iteration also ran a nested loop of length n.
hints: Big-O describes how resource usage grows as the input size grows.
Count how many times the halving loop executes.
Consider whether any memory grows with n.
idealAnswer: Big-O notation describes the asymptotic growth rate of an algorithm's resource usage (time or space) as the input size n grows. It captures the worst-case upper bound, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms so we can compare how algorithms scale. The halving loop runs approximately log2(n) times, so its time complexity is O(log n) and its space complexity is O(1), because only a single variable is used and no memory grows with n. If each iteration also ran a nested loop of length n, the time complexity would become O(n log n), since n units of work are done log2(n) times.
keyPoints: Big-O gives the worst-case asymptotic upper bound, dropping constants and lower-order terms.
The halving loop runs about log2(n) times, so its time complexity is O(log n).
No extra storage grows with the input, so space complexity is O(1).
A nested loop of length n inside each iteration would make the time complexity O(n log n).
Big-O matters for comparing scalability at large input sizes.

title: Hash Map vs Balanced Binary Search Tree
prompt: Compare using a hash map (hash table) versus a balanced binary search tree (such as an AVL tree or red-black tree) as the backing structure for a key-value store. Discuss the time complexity of lookup, insertion, and deletion, whether keys are kept in order, and memory considerations. Give an example situation where each would be the better choice.
hints: Think about average versus worst-case time complexity for each structure.
Consider whether keys can be iterated in sorted order.
Weigh the extra memory per node in a tree.
idealAnswer: A hash map offers average O(1) lookup, insertion, and deletion by hashing each key to a bucket, but it does not maintain any ordering of keys and can degrade to O(n) worst case under heavy collisions or a poor hash function. A balanced binary search tree guarantees O(log n) for lookup, insertion, and deletion, keeps keys in sorted order, and supports ordered traversal, predecessor/successor queries, and efficient range queries. The tradeoff is that each node carries extra overhead (key, value, child pointers, and balance/color metadata), so it uses more memory than a hash map for the same number of entries. Choose a hash map when you need the fastest average lookups and ordering does not matter, such as caching or counting frequencies. Choose a balanced BST when you need sorted iteration, range queries, or guaranteed worst-case bounds, such as an ordered map in a database or an autocomplete index.
keyPoints: Hash map: average O(1) operations, no key ordering, potential O(n) worst case under collisions.
Balanced BST: guaranteed O(log n) operations and keeps keys sorted.
BST supports range queries, predecessor/successor lookups, and sorted traversal.
BST uses more memory per entry (child pointers plus balance/color metadata).
Pick a hash map for speed without ordering; pick a balanced BST when ordering or range queries matter.
